t: the recitation of the Shema. Which consists of three passages from the Torah (detailed below, halachot 2-3), and begins with the words "Hear, O Israel."
as it says: when you lie down and when you rise. In the first two passages it is stated that one must speak of these matters at these times.
at the time when people usually lie down. At the time when people sleep.
stand. Rise from their sleep.
and they put first the reading of the passage Shema. This passage is said first among them.

the unity of the Name. A declaration that God alone is the Creator and Ruler of the world, and that His power is unlimited, as stated: "The Lord our God, the Lord is One" (see Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 1:1-7).
and the love of Him. That there is a commandment to love God, as stated there: "And you shall love the Lord your God." This love brings one to "a great desire to know the great Name" (ibid. 2:1-2).
and the study of Him. Studying knowledge of God, which brings one to love Him (see Hilchot Teshuvah 10:6).
for it is the great principle on which everything depends. That this is the most basic commandment, on which religion stands (see also Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 1:6, Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 14:2).
a command about the other commandments. A promise of reward for keeping them and punishment for neglecting them.

a command to remember all the commandments. That tzitzit are meant to remind of all the commandments, as it is written: "And you shall see it and remember all the commandments of the Lord..." (Numbers 15:39).
for the commandment of tzitzit does not apply at night. For it says of it "and you shall see it" - at the time of seeing, which is day (Hilchot Tzitzit 3:7).
all the days of your life. And the Sages expounded that the word "all" comes to include the nights.
he finishes the first verse. He completes "The Lord our God, the Lord is One."
and returns and reads as usual. Only "Blessed be the name..." is said quietly, and after it he returns to the continuation of the passage that he interrupted, and reads it normally.
and why do they read thus. And they add to the Shema a sentence that is not written in the Torah.

the way of the Lord in which Abraham and Isaac walked. That Abraham our forefather taught his children, as it says: "That he may command his children and his household after him, and they shall keep the way of the Lord, to do charity and justice" (Genesis 18:19; and see Hilchot De'ot 1:7).
lest there be a flaw among you. That among the children there might be one unfit to be included in the family.
whoever does not stand with me in the unity of the Master of the whole world. A person who does not join my faith in the unity of God.

in the matter that Moses our teacher told us. Just as in Moses' words to Israel, he addressed the possibility that there might be a man or a group "whose heart turns away today from the Lord our God, to go and serve the gods of those nations..."
hear from him. Listen to our declaration.
our father Israel. For this was the name of Jacob (Genesis 32:29; 35:10).
the elder. Jacob our forefather.
therefore all Israel are accustomed, etc.. In memory of that occasion, and because this sentence too contains acceptance of the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven.
he recites blessings before and after it. For the commandment of reciting the Shema, special blessings were instituted, as a preparation and a conclusion to the reading.
Yotzer Or. A blessing of praise for the creation of the luminaries, mentioning the praise that the angels give for the renewal of creation.
Ahavat Olam. Blessings of thanks for God's love of us, with requests relating to the study of Torah.
Emet VeYatziv... Emet Emunah. Blessings containing a declaration of God's unity and thanks for the redemption.
Ma'ariv Aravim. A blessing of praise for establishing the times of the day.
Hashkivenu. A blessing for protection during the night.
he opens it with Blessed. For these blessings begin with the formula "Blessed are You, Lord."
and concludes with Blessed. For they conclude with the formula "Blessed are You, Lord..."
and they have no opening. They do not begin with the formula Blessed, but with the blessing itself.
with all the other blessings, etc.. That is, all the blessings the Sages instituted.
Ezra and his court instituted them. At the beginning of the Second Temple period (for the reason for the enactment see Hilchot Tefillah 1:4).
and a person may not reduce them or add to them. In the wording of the blessing and its form (see also Hilchot Berakhot 1:5).
anyone who changes from the formula the Sages set. One who blesses not according to the pattern the Sages set for that blessing.

and anyone who does not say Emet VeYatziv in the morning and Emet Emunah in the evening. Who omitted these words from the text of the blessing, even though he said the rest of the blessing as instituted.
has not fulfilled his obligation. His obligation for this blessing, because these words are the essence of the blessing (compare Hilchot Berakhot 2:3).
because there is no order to the blessings. That the order is not essential.
for all blessings follow their conclusion. That the essence of the blessing is its conclusion, the blessing at the end.
the time of the recitation of the Shema at night. The time that is considered "when you lie down" (above 1).
from the time the stars come out. Which is about a third of an hour after sunset (Hilchot Terumot 7:2).
until midnight. The middle of the night.

before dawn rose. That he read before the time of dawn, which is the beginning of the lighting of the eastern sky before sunrise (about an hour and a fifth before it; Commentary on the Mishnah, Berakhot 1:1).

for they did not say until midnight, etc.. The Sages said that the time of the Shema is until midnight so that a person will not put off the fulfillment of the commandment and forget it, but will hasten to do it; but in truth its time lasts until dawn (for this principle see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 4:2).
sunrise. The beginning of the rising of the sun.
unless he was under duress. Although it is day (see below 12), in an emergency they rely on the fact that even at this time there are people who sleep.
he does not recite Hashkivenu. For this is not the time for beginning to lie down.
its commandment. The preferred time for reading it initially.
that he begin to read before sunrise. A short time before sunrise.

that he finish reading and recite the last blessing at sunrise. And he should place the conclusion of the last blessing, "Who redeemed Israel," right next to the morning prayer, as soon as its time arrives (Hilchot Tefillah 3:1, 7:17).
and this measure is about a tenth of an hour. The time it takes to read the Shema and its blessings is about six minutes.
its time. The time of reading.

until the end of three hours of the day. Until after three "seasonal hours" from the beginning of the day (whose length varies according to the length of the day), which is a quarter of the day. For until this time there are still people who rise from their sleep.
after dawn has risen. For even this time can be considered as day (for further examples see Hilchot Tefillah 3:7, Hilchot Milah 1:8, Hilchot Parah 11:1).
and in an emergency. When time is limited.
one who reads after three hours of the day. When the time of reading has already passed (above 11).
the obligation of reading the Shema at its time. For it must be read at the time of rising (above 1).
he is like one who reads the Torah. For this too is a commandment.
and he recites the blessings before and after it all day. For the blessings have no limited time and do not depend on the time of the Shema.
and did not direct his heart in the first verse. That he read it without attention to its meaning as a declaration of accepting the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven (see above 1:2).
even if he was reading, etc.. That he read the passages without connection to the commandment of reciting the Shema.
reads in the Torah as usual. That in the course of his study he reached those passages.
or proofreads the passages. Reads them from the text in order to correct them of errors.
at the time of the reading. At the proper time for the Shema.
they read as they are. In the manner in which they are at the time of reading, and there is no need to be in a particular position (compare Hilchot Tefillah 5:1-2).
lying with his face to the ground. Lying face down, because lying in these ways is not respectful (see also Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 21:19, Hilchot De'ot 4:5).
stops at the first verse. He pauses so that he will direct his heart to this verse (as stated above 1).
if he was sleeping, they wake him... until he reads the first verse. For it is the essence of the commandment (above 1).
from there on. After he has read the first verse (for a similar law see Hilchot Tefillah 7:2).
he stops until he reads the whole first passage. He stops his work for the first passage.
the artisans. Craftsmen employed by someone else.
so that the reading not be casual. As something not primary and important (see also below 8).
reads in his place. He need not come down, even though standing there interferes with concentration (compare Hilchot Tefillah 5:8).

and recites the blessings before and after it. For the blessings are connected with the reading (above 1:5; and see below 13), although they exempted artisans from certain blessings during their work (see Hilchot Tefillah 5:8, Hilchot Berakhot 2:2).
stops and reads. He stops his study (compare Hilchot Tefillah 6:8).
and he should read if time remains to read. That he should read afterward, if the time has not yet passed.
if he was eating... he finishes. He need not stop his activities, but reads after he finishes them.
and if he was afraid... this is praiseworthy. For he was zealous in the commandment. But there is no obligation to do so.
one who went down to immerse. After dawn, and the "time of its commandment" for the morning Shema has arrived, which ends at sunrise (above 1:11).
and if he was afraid that the sun would rise before he reads. That he will not have time to come out of the water and cover himself before sunrise.
he may cover himself with the water. For the water can be considered a covering, under conditions that will be explained.
he may not cover himself either with foul-smelling water. For it is forbidden to read in a place that has a bad smell (below 3:12).
nor with water for soaking. Water in which flax is soaked, which also stinks.
because his nakedness is visible through them. And it is forbidden to read facing nakedness (below 3:17).
in turbid water. Which is not transparent, and nakedness is not visible through it.
he may not signal with his eyes, nor wink with his lips, nor point with his fingers. That he not signal something to others, even without interrupting the speech.
a casual reading. As something not primary and important.
this is shameful. For he treats the commandment lightly.
and he must make his ear hear. He must read aloud until he hears his own words.
and if he did not make his ear hear, he has fulfilled his obligation. Whether he pronounced with his lips or blessed in his heart (Hilchot Berakhot 1:7).
to be precise in its letters. To be exact in reading them, as will be explained in the next halachah.
he must not soften the hard or harden the soft. He should not read letters with a dagesh as without one, or the reverse.
nor move the resting or rest the moving. He should not read a silent shva as a vocal shva, or the reverse.
therefore. Since one must be exact in the reading.
to leave a gap between any two similar letters, etc.. To pause slightly between them, so that they do not merge into one.
and he must articulate the zayin of tizkeru. To pronounce it clearly, so that it does not sound like a samekh.
and he must lengthen the dalet of echad, etc.. To pronounce it for a duration, so that he can then intend to proclaim Him King over the whole world.
and he must not rush the chet. That he not shorten its pronunciation, and as a result lengthen the aleph relatively.
ei chad. Which would mean "there is no one."
in any language that he knows. In any language that he understands.
he must be careful of corruptions of the words. That he translate the reading properly into that language, and be careful not to err in the translation in a way that corrupts the meaning.
and he is precise in that language, etc.. He must be exact in pronouncing it just as one is exact in the holy tongue.
out of order. Not in sequence.

because it is not adjacent to it in the Torah. For the passages of the Shema are not written consecutively in the Torah, and are not even said in the order in which they appear in the Torah (see above 1:2).
he read a verse and went back... this is shameful. For this is not respectful conduct, appearing to treat the dignity of the blessing lightly.
he read one word and repeated it... they silence him. For it appears as though he is addressing two authorities (see also Hilchot Tefillah 9:4).
in intervals. With pauses.

even if he waited between one interval and another long enough to finish all of it. Even a length of time sufficient for the entire reading does not require that he return to the beginning of the reading (compare Hilchot Tefillah 4:13).
in order. In sequence, and not out of order.
provided that he was alert at the first verse. For he must direct his intention in it (above 1).

if he is in doubt whether he read the Shema... he reads again and recites the blessings before and after it. For the reading is from the Torah, and a doubt about it is resolved stringently. And he reads it together with its blessings as instituted.
and he is in doubt whether he recited a blessing... he does not return and bless. For the blessings are not from the Torah, and a doubt about them is resolved leniently (see Hilchot Berakhot 8:12).
he lost track between one passage and another. He knows that he finished some section and does not know which.
he returns to the first chapter, which is Ve'ahavta. For he might be in the break before Ve'ahavta.
he returns to the beginning of the chapter. So that he will certainly read all of it.
he returns to Uchetavtem in Shema. Perhaps his place is there.
after he read: so that your days may increase. That he continued reading the verse that comes after "Uchetavtem" in "Vehayah im shamo'a."
for he goes by the habit of his tongue. Since he reached there, one must assume that by habit of his tongue he said the passages correctly.
and met others or they met him. He met other people and wants or needs to greet them.
between one chapter and another. Between the passages, as will be explained below 17.
he stops and begins and greets, etc.. He interrupts the reading, and he is permitted to initiate and greet them, even if they did not address him.
who met his father or his teacher or one greater than he in wisdom. Whom he is obligated to honor (Hilchot Mamrim 6:1, Hilchot Talmud Torah 5:1).
and he returns a greeting to anyone, etc.. That between the passages he may return a greeting even to one whom he is not obligated to honor, since the other initiated.
he fears him, such as a king or an oppressor. For refraining from greeting might lead to danger.
one whom he is obligated to honor... he stops and returns his greeting. For they are lenient about returning a greeting, since the other initiated.

but between Vayomer and Emet VeYatziv it is like the middle of the passage. For he must connect the words "the Lord your God" to the word "emet," so that the Shema too will conclude with acceptance of the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven (see Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 1:3-4).
and he may stop only to ask out of fear, etc.. As with the middle of a passage (above 16).
he may not delay its reading and go to look for water. He may not put off reading because of the need to look for water (compare Hilchot Tefillah 4:2-3).
he wipes his hands... with a pebble. Cleans them with stones.
in a bathhouse... in a privy. These are repulsive places, as will be explained below (and see Hilchot Tefillah 4:8).
in a cemetery... beside a corpse. One does not engage in sacred matters near a corpse or in a cemetery (see Hilchot Evel 14:13, Hilchot Tefillin 4:23, 10:6).
opposite it. Facing it and next to it.
but not inside it. For the place is repulsive from the very fact of its being prepared as a privy, even if it has not yet been used.
in a new bathhouse it is permitted to read inside it. Since it is not yet a repulsive place until it is used.
he designated one of them for a privy. They set it aside for this use.
and said of the second: and this one. This is not a definite expression of designation.
he said: and this one too. This is a definite expression of designation.
in a secular language. In a foreign language, not the holy tongue.
to think in his heart. To think without expressing it in speech.
secular matters. That are not matters of Torah or halachah.
it is permitted to say them in the holy tongue. There is no prohibition on speaking in the holy tongue in those places.
and likewise the epithets. The titles of the Holy One, blessed be He.

the special names, which are the names that are not erased. The holy names by which the Holy One, blessed be He, is called, whose erasure is forbidden (for the prohibition and the list of names see Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah 6:1-2).
and in an old bathhouse. That has been used (above 3).
to separate from a forbidden thing. To prevent a person from doing a forbidden act.
he separates him, even in the holy tongue and on sacred matters. He may tell him the law, even in the holy tongue.
and the excrement of dogs and pigs. Which are used in tanning hides.
when there are hides in them. For then they give off a foul smell.
but animal urine, they may read opposite it. For it is not so foul-smelling and repulsive.

a minor who cannot eat a k'zayit, etc.. An infant who cannot eat an olive-sized amount of grain food in the length of time in which an adult eats a grain food the size of three eggs, which is the measure of eating time for all matters in the Torah (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 14:8).
they need not distance themselves, etc.. For they are not so repulsive.
he should distance himself. Move away.
if they were in front of him he distances himself from them, etc.. He moves away from them until they are out of his line of sight (see Hilchot Tefillah 4:9).
in a level place. At the same height.
he sits beside the place and reads. And he need not move away.
for a separation has been made between them. For this is a different domain, even though there is no distance of four cubits between them.
he overturned a vessel. Turned a vessel upside down, which covers them completely.
like buried. Hidden and covered, as below 10.
even though he sees it, etc.. It is considered a partition, and there is no problem in the mere seeing of the excrement (compare below 16).
the urine of a single time. A single urination, and a revi'it of water neutralizes it.
in a pit. In a small hole in the ground.
he stands in his sandal over the hole. And the sandal serves as a partition.
a very small amount, such as a drop, he spits on it. For this amount can be covered by saliva.
a trace of excrement. Filth that has no substance.
it is permitted to read because it has no smell. And it is not in the category of excrement.
if it was in its place. In the anus.
because it is moist excrement, etc.. Even in a minute amount, since it is in its place.
a bad smell that has a source. That comes from something visible.
wind from below. Flatulence.
a vessel of dung and a chamber pot of urine. Vessels designated for excrement and urine.
for they are like a privy. In which it is forbidden to read even if it is clean (above 3).
floated. Drifted on the surface.
and a pig's mouth is like passing excrement. For it is always filthy.
he may not place his hands over his mouth and read. For this is not an effective partition.
until its stench has finished. Until the smell is gone.
this is permitted to read. For it is not customary to leave the filth in the house.
he was reading in the refuse heap. Which is a place where people were accustomed to relieve themselves.
but in case of doubt about urine, etc.. For the law of urine is more lenient (see also above 6).

so it is forbidden to read opposite nakedness. From the verse "and He shall not see in you an unseemly thing" (Deuteronomy 23:15), it is learned that one may not speak words of Torah facing nakedness.
until he turns his face. Until he turns his face to another direction and does not see it.
even a gentile or a minor. This does not depend on their being obligated in the commandments, but on the definition of nakedness.
and even if there was a glass partition. It does not help in this matter, since the prohibition concerns seeing (compare above 10).
and a woman's entire body is nakedness. In the parts of the body that are customarily covered.
opposite his own nakedness. His own nakedness (see above 2:7).
he had a cloth belt... on his loins. Which covers his nakedness but not the rest of his body.
so that his heel does not touch his nakedness. For even touch is forbidden like seeing.
he separates with his cloak below his heart. He divides, with the garment in which he is wrapped, between the heart and the nakedness.
he may not separate at his neck. In order to divide the head from the rest of the body.
because his heart sees the nakedness. And they must be separated during the reading (and see Hilchot Tefillah 4:7).
two who were sleeping in one cloak. And are not clothed.
until a cloak separates between them, etc.. The covering garment must be placed between the two, so that they are not found touching each other and come to impure thoughts.
their bodies are like his own and he does not feel them. For the contact does not cause him impure thought (see also Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 21:7).
he turns his face. Turns to another side.
provided that their form is like that of adults. On condition that their physical maturation has begun.
and afterwards he may not read, etc.. For their law is the same as that of others.
until the male is thirteen, etc.. From this age they are considered adults (Hilchot Ishut 2:1, 2:10).

women, slaves and minors are exempt from reciting the Shema. Women and slaves are exempt from commandments that are time-bound (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 12:3, Hilchot Chagigah 2:1), and minors are not obligated in the commandments from the Torah until they become adults (for their definition see Hilchot Ishut 2:10 ff.).

in order to train them in the commandments. This is an obligation from the Sages, to accustom minors to the commandments (for further examples see Hilchot Tefillin 4:13, Hilchot Tzitzit 3:9, Hilchot Berakhot 5:1 and others).
one whose mind is troubled and hurried, etc.. His mind was not at ease because of that matter.
lest he not find signs of virginity. Lest he find that she is not a virgin (see Hilchot Ishut 11:9).
and if he delayed until the end of Shabbat. That is, four days, since a virgin marries on Wednesday (ibid. 10:15).
for his mind has cooled and his heart has become coarse toward her. He has calmed down and is no longer so excited.
for he is engaged in a commandment. For marriage involves the commandment of being fruitful and multiplying.
and he has nothing that disturbs his mind. He is no longer anxious that she may not be found a virgin.
a dead person for whom he is obligated to mourn. Relatives of the first degree (see Hilchot Evel 2:1-2).

is exempt from the recitation of the Shema until he buries him. And likewise exempt from all the commandments of the Torah (Hilchot Evel 4:6; and see Hilchot Tefillah 6:10 regarding exemption from prayer).
even if he is not his own dead, etc.. Who is not his relative, he is exempt because he is engaged in a commandment.
and the second slips away to another place and reads. For he is not needed for guarding. He must go to another place because one may not read beside the dead (above 3:2).
they do not take out the dead for burial close to the time of the Shema. So as not to prevent the escorts from reading at its time.
a great man. Important and honored.
and they are escorting the dead. While they are engaged in the funeral.
and their replacements and the replacements of their replacements. All those who are meant to replace them in carrying the bier.
when the dead is placed before them. And they cannot read in its presence (as above 3).
and silent. Quiet and does not read with them.
and the mourners returned to receive consolation. They went to the place where people stand and console them.
to form a line to receive consolation. The comforters stand before the mourners row after row, and one by one pass before the mourners and console them (Hilchot Evel 13:1-2).
to begin and finish even one verse, etc.. During the walk from the grave to the line.
that they may take leave. That they may part.
the inner ones. Those standing in the inner row, closest to the mourners.
provided that his mind is settled. That his mind is free for the reading (compare Hilchot Tefillah 4:15).

all the impure are obligated... even though they could rise from their impurity, etc.. Impurity does not prevent the reading at all, even if there is the possibility of purifying oneself from it and reading in a state of purity (see also Hilchot Berakhot 1:9).
and Ezra and his court enacted that a ba'al keri may not read, etc.. The reason for this enactment was to restrain the people from excessive marital relations (Hilchot Tefillah 4:4-5).
and this enactment did not spread among all Israel, and most of the community had no power to uphold it. The enactment did not spread throughout Israel, because they were not able to keep it.
therefore it was annulled. For this is the law for an enactment that did not spread among most of the community (Hilchot Mamrim 2:6).
and they are ba'alei keri'in. While they are impure with the impurity of keri, without having immersed (and see further Hilchot Tefillah 4:6).
